title: Python Tutorial: From First Line to Small Projects
subtitle: Learn Python by doing: values, loops, lists, functions, classes and more, with a lab in every chapter
author: Lilith Learning Lab
description: A hands-on Python tutorial for beginners. You will learn variables and types, numbers and strings, decisions, loops, lists and tuples, dictionaries and sets, functions, comprehensions, errors, classes, modules and generators, then combine them in small projects. Every chapter has a short ELI5 block, a quiz and Python labs that run on the built-in interpreter, so you can practise without installing anything.

chapters.title: Hello, Python

maps.title: Basics
links: Program | is | A list of instructions

summary: Python is a language for giving a computer instructions. You write lines, and the interpreter runs them top to bottom.
A variable is a name for a value. The equals sign puts a value into a name.
Every value has a type, such as int, float, str or bool.

glossary.def: The program that reads and runs your Python code.
A name that points to a value.
The kind of a value, like int or str.
A function that shows values.
Text after # that Python ignores.
Giving a name a value with =.

keyPoints: Lines run from top to bottom.
name = value creates or changes a variable.
print(a, b) shows values separated by spaces.
type(x) tells you the type.
Names use letters, digits and underscores, and cannot start with a digit.
A # starts a comment.

items: ELI5. Python is a way to write instructions so a computer can follow them. A variable is a sticky label on a box that holds a thing.
A program is a recipe. The computer follows each line in order. Python reads easily, so many people start with it. You can try every example in the practice area of this course.

lesson.code:
print('Hello, world!')
name = 'Ada'
age = 36
print(name, 'is', age)
print(type(name), type(age))

items: A variable is a label stuck on a box. The line age = 36 puts the number 36 in a box labelled age. Later lines can read the box or replace what is inside. Choose clear names, like total_price, so you can read your program later.

Python has a few basic types. An int is a whole number. A float has a decimal point. A str is text in quotes. A bool is True or False. The function type tells you which one a value is. Mixing them wrongly causes an error, which is Python's way of telling you something is off.

lesson.code:
x = 5          # int
y = 2.5        # float
z = '5'        # str, not a number
print(x + y)   # 7.5
print(z + z)   # 55, text joined
print(x + z)   # TypeError

items: Errors are normal. Python prints the line and the kind of problem. Read the last line first. Fixing errors is a large part of programming, and each one teaches you something.

chapters.title: Numbers and strings
summary: Python does arithmetic with + - * / and more: // for whole division, % for the remainder and ** for powers.
A string is text. You can join strings, repeat them, pick characters by index and cut pieces with slices.
Strings have methods such as upper, split, replace and strip.

glossary.def: // divides and drops the fraction.
% gives the remainder after division.
A position in a string or list, starting at 0.
A part cut out with s[start:stop].
A function attached to a value, like s.upper().
Cannot be changed in place; strings are immutable.

keyPoints: Dividing with / always gives a float.
s[0] is the first character; s[-1] is the last.
s[1:4] gives characters 1, 2 and 3.
Strings never change; methods return new strings.
round(x, 2) rounds to 2 decimals.

items: ELI5. Numbers are for counting and strings are for words. A string is a necklace of letters, and you can pick out one bead or a few.

Python is a fine calculator. Plus, minus, times and divide work as you expect. The slash gives a float, even for 6 / 3. Two slashes give a whole-number result. The percent sign gives the remainder, which is handy for questions like is this number even.
A string is a row of characters. Counting starts at zero, so the first character is at index 0. Negative indexes count from the end. A slice takes a part. The start is included and the stop is not.

lesson.code:
s = 'Python'
print(s[0], s[-1])   # P n
print(s[1:4])        # yth
print(s[:2], s[2:])  # Py thon
print(len(s))        # 6
print(s.upper())     # PYTHON

items: Strings come with many methods. Split breaks text into a list of words. Join puts a list back together. Replace swaps one piece for another. Strip removes spaces at the ends. Because strings cannot change, each method gives you a new string and leaves the old one alone.

lesson.code:
words = 'a,b,c'.split(',')   # ['a', 'b', 'c']
print('-'.join(words))          # a-b-c
print('  hi  '.strip())         # hi
print('cat'.replace('c', 'b'))  # bat
print('Hello %s, you are %d' % ('Ada', 36))

cards.q: Can a string change in place?

chapters.title: Making decisions
summary: An if statement runs a block of code only when a condition is True. Add elif and else for other cases.
Conditions come from comparisons like == != < > <= >=, joined with and, or and not.
Indentation, four spaces, shows which lines belong to the block.

glossary.def: An expression that is True or False.
Indented lines that belong to an if, loop or function.
Short for else if: another condition to try.
A value treated as True: non-zero numbers and non-empty things.
0, empty text, empty list and None count as False.
x if cond else y: a one-line choice.

keyPoints: == compares; = assigns.
Python checks if, then each elif, then else, and runs the first match only.
and needs both True; or needs one; not flips.
Chained comparisons work: 0 < x < 10.
Empty values are falsy.
Indent with four spaces and stay consistent.

items: ELI5. An if is a fork in the road. The computer asks a yes-or-no question and walks down the matching path.

Programs make choices. The if statement asks a question, and the lines indented below it run only if the answer is True. Python uses the indent itself to know where a block starts and ends, so spacing matters.

A comparison gives True or False. Use == to ask if two values are equal. A single = would assign instead, which is a classic mistake. You can join conditions with and, or and not. Python lets you chain, so 0 < x < 10 means what it looks like.

Python also treats some values as True or False on their own. Zero, empty text, an empty list and None count as False. Everything else counts as True. That lets you write if items: to mean if the list has anything in it.

lesson.code:
x = 7
print(0 < x < 10)          # True
print(x > 5 and x % 2 == 0) # False
label = 'big' if x > 5 else 'small'
print(label)
if []:
    print('never')

practice.intro: Write leap(year): True if divisible by 4, except years divisible by 100 unless also divisible by 400.
practice.solution:

    return year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)

chapters.title: Loops
summary: A for loop repeats code for each item in a sequence. A while loop repeats as long as a condition is True.
range(n) gives the numbers 0 to n minus 1. break leaves a loop early and continue skips to the next round.
A common pattern is an accumulator: start with an empty total, then add to it in each round.

glossary.def: Code that repeats.
To go through items one at a time.
A sequence of numbers: range(start, stop, step).
A variable that builds up a result in a loop.
Ends the loop right away.
A loop whose condition never becomes False.

keyPoints: for x in items: runs once per item.
while cond: repeats; make sure something changes.
break exits; continue jumps to the next round.
enumerate(items) gives index and item.
Loops can sit inside loops.

items: ELI5. A loop is doing the same chore again and again, like putting each toy in the box one by one until the floor is clear.

Computers are good at repeating. A for loop takes each item of a sequence in turn and runs its block with that item. The word range makes a sequence of numbers, so you can repeat something a set number of times.
A while loop repeats as long as its condition holds. You must change something inside, or it never stops. Use break to leave early, for example when you find what you were looking for.

lesson.code:
n = 27
steps = 0
while n != 1:
    n = n // 2 if n % 2 == 0 else 3 * n + 1
    steps += 1
print(steps)   # 111

for i, ch in enumerate('abc'):
    print(i, ch)

items: Loops can nest. A loop inside a loop runs its full set for each round of the outer one. That is how you build tables and grids. Pick the loop that matches the job: for when you know the items, while when you wait for a condition.

chapters.title: Lists and tuples
summary: A list holds items in order and can change. Square brackets make one, and you reach items by index.
Lists have methods: append, pop, insert, remove, sort and more. Slices copy parts.
A tuple is like a list that cannot change. Use it for small fixed groups, like a point.

glossary.def: An ordered, changeable collection.
An ordered, fixed collection in parentheses.
Can be changed after creation.
Adds an item to the end of a list.
Splitting a sequence into names: a, b = pair.
Two names for the same list; changing one changes both.

keyPoints: items = [3, 1, 2]; items[0] is 3.
append adds, pop removes the last, insert and remove work by place and value.
sorted(items) returns a new list; items.sort() changes in place.
len, sum, min and max work on lists.
b = a makes an alias; b = a[:] or list(a) makes a copy.
Tuples: (1, 2); unpack with x, y = point.

items: ELI5. A list is a row of boxes with numbers on the front. A tuple is the same row, but taped shut.
A list is a row of boxes, each with a position. Make one with square brackets. You can change items, add more and remove some. The same indexing and slicing rules as strings work here.

lesson.code:
nums = [5, 3, 8]
nums.append(1)      # [5, 3, 8, 1]
nums[0] = 9         # [9, 3, 8, 1]
print(nums[1:3])    # [3, 8]
print(len(nums), sum(nums), max(nums))
print(sorted(nums)) # new sorted list

items: Beware of aliases. The line b = a does not copy the list. It gives the same list a second name, so a change through b shows up in a. To make a real copy, use a slice with nothing in it, or the list function.

A tuple is a list you promise not to change. It is written with parentheses and is good for things that belong together, like a point with x and y. You can unpack a tuple into separate names in one line. Functions often return tuples to give back several values at once.

lesson.code:
point = (3, 4)
x, y = point
print(x, y)
first, *rest = [1, 2, 3]
print(first, rest)   # 1 [2, 3]
names = ['bo', 'al']
names.sort()
print(names)

quiz.q: What does b = a do to a list?

practice.title: Running total
practice.intro: Write running(nums): a list where each item is the sum of all numbers up to that point.
practice.hint: Keep a total and append it.
practice.solution:
def running(nums):
    out = []
    t = 0
    for n in nums:
        t += n
        out.append(t)
    return out

chapters.title: Dictionaries and sets
summary: A dictionary stores pairs: a key and its value. You look things up by key, and lookups are fast.
Methods such as get, items, keys and values help you read a dict. Keys must be unchangeable, like text, numbers or tuples.
A set holds unique items and supports union, intersection and difference.

glossary.def: A collection of key and value pairs.
The label used to look a value up.
A collection with no duplicates and no order.
All items from both sets.
Items in both sets.
Unchangeable enough to be a key.

keyPoints: d.get('z', 0) gives 0 if missing; d['z'] would raise KeyError.
for k, v in d.items() visits each pair.
'a' in d tests for a key.
Sets: {1, 2}; set(list) removes duplicates.
a | b union, a & b intersection, a - b difference.

items: ELI5. A dictionary is a phone book: you look up a name and get a number. A set is a bag where every toy must be different.
A list finds things by position. A dictionary finds them by name. It is like a phone book: look up a name and get a number. Each key appears once, and each key has one value.

lesson.code:
ages = {'ada': 36, 'bo': 25}
ages['cy'] = 41
print(ages['ada'])          # 36
print(ages.get('zed', 0))   # 0
for name, age in ages.items():
    print(name, age)
print('bo' in ages)         # True

items: Counting is a classic use. Walk through the items, and for each one add one to its count in a dictionary. The get method with a default of zero makes this short, because a missing key counts as zero.

A set is a bag of unique items. Adding something twice has no effect. Sets are fast at asking whether an item is in the bag, and they do the maths of overlap: union, intersection and difference. Use a set to remove duplicates, or to compare two groups.

quiz.q: How do you read a key safely?
What does a set not allow?

chapters.title: Functions

maps.title: Functions
links: Default | fills in | A missing argument

summary: A function is a named block of code you can run again and again. def starts it, and return sends a value back.
Parameters are names for the inputs. Default values make some inputs optional.
Names made inside a function are local to it. A function can call itself, which is called recursion.

glossary.def: A named, reusable block of code.
A name for an input in the definition.
The actual value passed in a call.
Ends the function and gives back a value.
Where a name can be seen.
A function that calls itself on a smaller problem.

keyPoints: def name(params): then an indented body.
A function without return gives back None.
def f(x, y=10): y is optional.
Call with names: f(1, y=2).
Variables made inside are local.
A recursive function needs a base case that stops it.

items: ELI5. A function is a little machine. You put things in, it does its job, and it hands you back a result you can use again.
When you notice you are writing the same lines twice, make a function. A function has a name, takes inputs and gives back a result. The def line defines it. Nothing runs until you call it.

lesson.code:
def area(w, h=1):
    """Area of a rectangle."""
    return w * h

print(area(3, 4))    # 12
print(area(5))       # 5
print(area(h=2, w=6))# 12

items: Variables made inside a function live only there. This is called local scope. It keeps functions tidy, because they cannot damage each other's names by accident. Pass things in as parameters and send them back with return.
A function can call itself. This is recursion. It works when a problem contains a smaller copy of itself. You must give a base case, a simple input that returns right away, or the calls never end.

Good functions do one thing, have a clear name and avoid surprises. A docstring, the text in triple quotes just under def, explains what the function does. Small functions are easy to test, and you can combine them into bigger programs.

quiz.q: What does a function without return give back?
What does a base case do?
Where is a local variable visible?

chapters.title: Comprehensions and functional tools

maps.title: Comprehensions
links: Comprehension | builds | A list in one line
sorted key | orders | By a rule

summary: A list comprehension builds a list in one line: [x * 2 for x in nums if x > 0]. It reads like a sentence.
lambda makes a tiny unnamed function. sorted, min and max accept a key function.
zip pairs up sequences, and any and all test whole lists.

glossary.def: A short way to build a list, dict or set from a loop.
A small anonymous function.
A function that tells sorted what to compare.
Pairs up items from several sequences.
True if at least one item is True.
True if every item is True.

keyPoints: [expr for x in items if cond] makes a list.
{k: v for ...} makes a dict; {x for ...} makes a set.
lambda x: x * 2 is a function.
sorted(items, key=len) sorts by length.
zip(a, b) pairs items by position.
any(...) and all(...) test conditions.

items: ELI5. A comprehension is a quick recipe: take every item, maybe skip some, and change each one, all in one sentence.

Many loops just build a new list from an old one. A comprehension does that in one line. Read it from left to right: give me expr for each x in items, if cond. It is shorter and often clearer than a loop with append.

lesson.code:
nums = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]
squares = [n * n for n in nums]
evens = [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
lookup = {n: n * n for n in nums}
print(squares, evens)
print(lookup[3])   # 9

items: A lambda is a function with no name, written in one line. It is handy as a key for sorting. If you sort words by length, the key function tells sorted how to measure each word.

lesson.code:
words = ['pear', 'fig', 'banana']
print(sorted(words, key=len))
print(sorted(words, key=lambda w: w[-1]))
print(max(words, key=len))
names = ['a', 'b']
scores = [10, 20]
print(list(zip(names, scores)))

items: The functions any and all check a whole list at once. Any is True if one item passes. All is True only if every item passes. Together with a comprehension, they say a lot in a few words.

quiz.q: What does [n*2 for n in nums] do?

cards.a: True if one item is True.

cards.q: Can you make a dict with a comprehension?

practice.title: Dot product
practice.intro: Write dot(a, b): multiply matching items of two lists and add them up.

chapters.title: Errors and exceptions
summary: When something goes wrong Python raises an exception. If nothing handles it, the program stops and prints a traceback.
try and except let you handle an error and carry on. raise lets your own code signal a problem.
Catch the specific error you expect, not everything.

glossary.def: An object that signals something went wrong.
The report of where the error happened.
A block of code that may fail.
A block that runs when a named error happens.
Starts an exception on purpose.
A block that always runs at the end.

keyPoints: Common errors: ValueError, TypeError, KeyError, IndexError, ZeroDivisionError.
try: ... except ValueError: ... handles one kind.
except Exception as e: gives you the error object.
raise ValueError('message') makes your own.
finally runs whether or not an error happened.
Read tracebacks from the bottom up.

items: ELI5. An error is the computer saying it got confused. A try block is a safety net that catches it so the program keeps going.

Errors happen: a file is missing, someone types text instead of a number, you divide by zero. Python stops with a message called a traceback. Read it from the bottom: the last line names the error, and the lines above show where.
Catch only what you expect. A bare except hides bugs, because it also swallows mistakes you did not plan for. Name the error type. The finally block runs no matter what, which is good for cleanup.

Your own code can raise errors too. If a function gets input that makes no sense, raise a ValueError with a clear message rather than returning a wrong answer quietly. Failing early and loudly makes bugs easier to find.

cards.q: Why name the error in except?

chapters.title: Classes and objects

maps.title: Classes
links: Method | is | A function in a class

summary: A class is a blueprint, and an object is one thing built from it. Objects bundle data (attributes) and behaviour (methods).
The __init__ method sets up a new object. Every method takes self, the object it works on.
A class can inherit from another to reuse and change its behaviour.

glossary.def: A blueprint for objects.
One instance made from a class.
A variable stored on an object.
A function defined inside a class.
The object a method is working on.
A class taking on the features of another.

keyPoints: class Name: starts a class.
def __init__(self, ...): runs when you create an object.
self.x = x stores an attribute.
obj.method() calls a method.
class Dog(Animal): inherits from Animal.
Methods can be overridden in the child class.

items: ELI5. A class is a cookie cutter and each object is a cookie. Every cookie has its own icing, but all share the same shape.

So far you have used built-in types like lists and strings. A class lets you make your own. Think of a class as a cookie cutter and an object as a cookie. You describe once what a thing has and what it can do, and then make as many as you like.

The method named __init__ runs when you make a new object. The first parameter, self, is the object itself. Attributes you set on self stay with that object. Every method receives self first, so it can read and change the object's data.
Inheritance lets a new class start from an old one. The child class gets all the parent's attributes and methods and can change or add some. It models the idea that a dog is a kind of animal.

Use classes when data and the actions on it belong together, such as a bank account with a balance and deposit and withdraw. For simple jobs a function or a dict is often enough. Choose the simplest tool that keeps your program clear.

cards.q: What can a child class do?

chapters.title: Modules, iterators and generators

maps.title: Modules
links: Module | is | A file of code
Iterator | gives | One item at a time

summary: A module is a file of Python code you load with import. Python ships with a large standard library: math, random, json, datetime and more.
An iterator hands out items one at a time. A generator is a function that uses yield to make one.
Generators are lazy: they make each value only when asked, so they can be very long, even endless.

glossary.def: A file of code you can import.
Loads a module so you can use it.
The modules that come with Python.
An object that gives items one at a time.
A function that yields values lazily.
Gives a value and pauses the function.

keyPoints: import math; math.sqrt(16) is 4.0.
from math import pi imports one name.
json.dumps and json.loads turn data to text and back.
A for loop works on anything iterable.
yield pauses a function and gives a value.
next(gen) asks a generator for its next value.

items: ELI5. A module is a toolbox someone else packed for you. A generator is a vending machine that gives one snack each time you press the button.

You do not have to write everything yourself. A module is a file of finished code. The import line loads it, and then you use its names with a dot. Python includes hundreds of modules in its standard library.

lesson.code:
import math
print(math.sqrt(16), math.pi)
from math import floor
print(floor(2.7))   # 2
import json
text = json.dumps({'a': [1, 2]})
print(text)
print(json.loads(text)['a'])

items: A for loop works on anything you can iterate over, and an iterator is the thing doing the handing out. A list holds all its items at once. A generator makes each item only when asked. That saves memory and can even describe an endless sequence.

The keyword yield is like return that remembers its place. The function pauses at the yield, gives a value, and picks up from the same spot on the next request. Generator expressions look like comprehensions with round brackets, and work lazily too.

lesson.code:
squares = (n * n for n in range(1000000))
print(next(squares), next(squares))
print(sum(n for n in range(10)))   # 45

keyPoints: Start with the smallest working version.
Write a function for each idea.
Test with simple, edge and large inputs.
Print or log values to see what the code does.
Read error messages carefully.
Improve names and remove repetition only after it works.

items: ELI5. Big jobs get easier when you cut them into small pieces, test each piece, and then snap them together like building blocks.

A big problem is easier when you cut it into small ones. To analyse a text file you might write one function to split it into words, one to count them and one to report the top results. Each piece is small enough to test alone.

Test early and often. Try a normal case, an empty input, a single item and a surprising one. Many bugs hide at the edges. When a result looks wrong, print the values in the middle to see where it went off.

Do not worry about writing perfect code the first time. Make it work, then make it clear. Rename confusing variables, split long functions and remove repeated lines. Because you tested it, you can change it with confidence.

Where to go next? Read other people's code, build small tools for your own needs and use the Python documentation. Learn the libraries for your goals: data, web, games or automation. The best way to learn is to build something you care about.
